text:
Introduction

The Building Safety (Remediation of Unsafe Cladding etc) Bill

Everyone deserves to live in a decent, safe, secure and affordable home. Yet 9 years after the Grenfell Tower Tragedy, there are still too many buildings with unsafe cladding. The building safety crisis continues to endanger lives, leaving people stuck in unsafe homes they are unable to sell.

The Building Safety Act 2022 ensured developers could be held to account and protected most leaseholders from substantial building safety costs. However, progress in identifying and remediating buildings with unsafe cladding has been inconsistent. In some cases, legal framework gaps have made it difficult to identify those responsible for buildings and ensure timely action.

The government set out its plans to improve remediation in the Remediation Acceleration Plan in December 2024, and the Update to the Remediation Acceleration Plan in July 2025. These had 3 objectives:

identify all buildings with unsafe cladding

fix buildings faster

support residents

This bill will deliver on the legislative commitments of the Remediation Acceleration Plan.

This bill’s objectives are to:

create certainty of which buildings require cladding remediation and to what standard

give regulators the powers they need to hold the worst blockers to account, ensuring those responsible for fixing historic and ongoing failures do so more quickly

make the companies that made unsafe building products contribute to fix the problems they caused

ensure all residents have a route to remediation, and that no building is left behind

This guide summarises the bill’s reforms. As such, it is a practical companion to the bill. The bill’s Explanatory Notes provide clause-by-clause commentary on the measures.

Summary of key objectives

The Building Safety (Remediation of Unsafe Cladding etc) Bill will:

1. Create certainty of which buildings require cladding remediation and to what standard

It is essential that we are clear about the scale of unsafe cladding. The bill will introduce a register of all residential, 11 to 18 metre-high buildings in England. It will also require those responsible for these buildings to assess them for fire-safety risks within twelve months of the legislation coming into force. The bill will mandate a consistent approach for Fire Risk Assessments of External Walls (FRAEWs) and compel auditing so FRAEWs are carried out properly.

2. Give regulators the powers they need to hold the worst blockers to account, ensuring those responsible for fixing historic and ongoing failures do so more quickly

To work effectively, the current system must be strengthened and underpinned with effective sanctions to incentivise action. The bill’s legal duty will require those responsible to remediate residential buildings over 11 metres high, in line with recommendations in FRAEWs. Regulators will be able to act against those delaying remediation, including criminal prosecution for the worst cases, and require information on building ownership to help identify and pursue those responsible. Other measures will improve co-operation and accountability between the various regulators.

3. Make the companies that made unsafe building products contribute to fix the problems they caused

The government has committed £5.15 billion to remediate buildings in England; and the cost to the 53 developers who have signed the Developer Remediation Contract is estimated at £4.2 billion. Construction product manufacturers have yet to contribute. The bill will make it easier for a claim to be brought against a manufacturer who has supplied unsafe construction products. It will also expand the pool of parties who can bring a claim, including to developers.

4. Ensure all residents have a route to remediation, and that no building is left behind

The current system lacks legal mechanisms to ensure remediation work is completed where those responsible for a building are absent or determined to ignore their building safety obligations. The bill will introduce a last-resort backstop mechanism to allow a public authority to carry out remediation work themselves. Through remediation management orders, a tribunal may allow a relevant authority to take control of works and recover costs from the responsible party.

The bill also contains amendments to previous legislation, designed to protect residents and ensure there are routes to remediation where building ownership is unclear, absent or negligent.

Some bill measures will require secondary legislation for implementation. We anticipate that secondary legislation will be made within one year of Royal Assent.

The legal duty to remediate

Overview

Building owners have always been responsible for making their buildings safe. However, there is currently no clear legal duty on those responsible to remediate unsafe cladding specifically. The current approach requires building-by-building enforcement action and only results in penalties once failure to comply with a statutory notice has been prosecuted. This process creates capacity and regulatory bottlenecks, and is slow, costly and often litigious.

The bill will introduce a clear legal duty on responsible entities of medium and high-rise buildings to assess and remediate life-critical external wall fire safety risks. Failure to comply, without reasonable excuse, will be an offence with potential financial and custodial sanctions.

The legal duty to remediate will apply to multi-occupied residential buildings in England over 11 metres in height or with at least 5 storeys, completed before 28 June 2022. It will apply to private and social sector buildings, including enfranchised and commonhold buildings. However, buildings subject to the developer remediation contract will be excluded from the legal duty to remediate because equivalent requirements are already in place. Under the developer remediation contract, developers have committed to assess and remediate life-critical fire safety defects in buildings for which they are responsible, where remediation is necessary. The developer remediation contract is supported by the Responsible Actors Scheme, under which eligible developers risk severe commercial consequences if they fail to meet their remediation obligations. More information is available: Developer remediation contract.

The legal duty to remediate will fall on parties with the relevant repairing obligation for the building (the ‘responsible entity’). This may include freeholders, leaseholders in a head or sub-lease, right to manage companies, or resident management companies.

Local authorities, fire and rescue authorities, and the Building Safety Regulator will have a duty to enforce the legal duty to remediate. The purpose of the bill is to ensure that buildings are remediated, not to penalise those who are engaging constructively and making reasonable progress. Regulators will have discretion over the most appropriate response in individual cases, including the use of new civil and criminal sanctions or statutory notices and orders under existing regimes.

Homes England will undertake these audit functions across England, including in London. The Mayor of London has agreed that Homes England should exercise these audit functions directly in London and not through delegation. This arrangement is limited to the specific audit functions established by the bill and does not affect or delegate any other Mayoral functions or responsibilities in the Greater London area.

Duty to assess

We believe there are still buildings with unsafe cladding that remain unidentified, particularly those between 11 and 18 metres. The bill will introduce a legal duty to assess, so that unsafe buildings are identified and the work needed to fix them is clearly established.

Responsible entities will need to assess their buildings for fire safety risks within a fixed period – between 16 May 2022 and the date 12 months after Royal Assent. This will involve commissioning an FRAEW, where recommended by a fire risk assessment. The 16 May 2022 start date reflects when the Fire Safety Act 2021 came into force. This clarified that fire risk assessments must consider external walls, structure and flat entrance doors in buildings containing 2 or more sets of domestic premises.

The bill will require FRAEWs to follow the PAS 9980 methodology (this will be set out in regulations). PAS 9980 is industry guidance produced by the British Standards Institution and already widely used, including in government remediation programmes. Making PAS 9980 a legal requirement will establish a clear, standardised approach to assessing external walls and support enforcement of the duties to assess, mitigate and remediate.

In most cases, buildings will have already been assessed. Where a building has been assessed between 16 May 2022 and the bill coming into force, the assessment will not need to be repeated if it complied with the requirements in force at the time. This includes buildings in government remediation schemes.

The bill will also introduce mandatory auditing of FRAEWs. All assessments that recommend mitigation or remediation will need to be submitted to Homes England for audit by the assessment deadline. Homes England will also have the power – for the first time – to audit a proportion of FRAEWs that conclude no work is necessary. Auditing will support consistency and quality and provide a clear, agreed understanding of the remediation required for each building.

The assessment duty will be backed by new enforcement powers. Failure to carry out an assessment within the required timeframe, without a reasonable excuse, will be a criminal offence. This could result in a criminal prosecution or escalating financial penalties, to deter continuing non-compliance. Responsible entities will have the right to appeal any criminal convictions and financial penalties.

Remediation Compliance Plans

Where an FRAEW recommends remedial work, responsible entities will be required to produce a Remediation Compliance Plan by the date 15 months from Royal Assent. The plan must set out:

the steps that the responsible entity proposes to take to carry out the recommendations in a fire risk assessment to remediate and/or take interim measures in relation to the external walls of the building

the timetable in accordance with which the responsible entity proposes to take those steps

where the responsible entity is a company, information identifying the director responsible for ensuring compliance with remediation duties, details of any beneficial owners, and information about the responsible entity’s portfolio and wider corporate group

The Remediation Compliance Plan must be published on their website and proactively shared with residents and leaseholders. Responsible entities will not be able to pass on the cost of producing the Remediation Compliance Plan to qualifying leaseholders. Failure to publish a Remediation Compliance Plan by the statutory deadline will result in substantial financial penalties that continue to accrue until the plan is produced.

Legal duty to remediate and mitigate

Even where unsafe buildings are known, progress can be slow, and too often residents are left stuck in expensive interim arrangements for years. An unacceptably high number of buildings identified with unsafe cladding have not yet started or completed remediation. In many cases, enforcement action and litigation has been required to progress works.

The legal duty to remediate will make clear who is responsible for remediation, what is required of them, and that inaction will not be tolerated. The bill will place a clear legal duty on responsible entities to permanently remediate unsafe cladding on their buildings by carrying out the recommendations in an FRAEW, and implementing any recommended interim measures, as soon as reasonably practicable.

The department will publish regulations and statutory guidance to support responsible entities to comply with their legal duties. We will set out what may be considered a ‘required remediation step’, such as an application to the Cladding Safety Scheme, and what may be considered ‘as soon as reasonably practicable’ to take each step. Responsible entities will be required to set out their proposed steps and indicative timelines in their Remediation Compliance Plan and will be held to account for these commitments.

Where a responsible entity deliberately fails to mitigate or take steps to remediate fire safety risks at 11 metres plus buildings as soon as reasonably practicable, they will be liable for criminal prosecution and, if convicted, up to 2 years in prison. As an alternative to prosecution, regulators may issue a financial penalty of up to £500,000. To make sure responsible entities are not unfairly penalised for delays beyond their control – such as severe supply chain issues or contractor shortages – the bill will introduce a ‘reasonable excuse’ defence to safeguard those who are acting in good faith. Responsible entities who are freeholders will not be able to pass on penalty costs to leaseholders.

Where a responsible entity is a company and their failure to meet remediation duties is due to the consent, connivence or neglect of a director, then enforcing authorities will be able to prosecute a director for a criminal offence. The directors responsible for ensuring that a corporate responsible entity complies with its remediation duties will be identified by the Remediation Compliance Plan.

There is remediation funding in place for all work required by the legal duty to remediate.

Obstruction offence

Remediation work can be delayed as a result of disputes over access to buildings, scope of works, or contractual arrangements. The Remediation Bill will create a new offence where someone unreasonably obstructs any person who is lawfully assessing or fixing a building with serious external fire safety risks.

In practice, this could mean obstructing:

responsible entities under the legal duty to remediate

developers who have signed the Developer Remediation Contract and committed to carry out works under it

third parties (for example, contractors or managing agents) who have taken on responsibility for remediation, including through litigation or settlement

remediation authorities using their powers under the new Remediation Backstop

Examples of obstruction could include:

refusing or delaying access to the building for safety assessments or works

refusing or delaying granting a third-party permission to carry out works to a building

raising unreasonable disputes about the need for or scope of the remediation works

However, not all disputes are obstruction. Often disputes arise from concerns in good faith, for example about safety, access, or the scope of works. Often the parties involved will work constructively to resolve them. To ensure that valid disputes are not penalised, the bill will include a ‘reasonable excuse’ defence.

If an individual is found to be obstructing assessment or remediation, they will be liable for a fine of up to £40,000. If the obstruction is committed by a company, they could be subject to a penalty based on their worldwide revenue.

Fines on parent entities under the legal duty to remediate

In some cases, the legal responsibility for remediating unsafe buildings will lie with a single company that is part of a wider corporate group. These structures can mean that the company with the formal responsibility for a building has limited assets, while financial resources and decision-making sit elsewhere in the group.

This can create a risk that those who ultimately control and benefit from a building can avoid the consequences of non-compliance with the legal duty to remediate. Companies may use subsidiaries or special purpose vehicles with limited capital to hold freeholds or repairing obligations, reducing the effectiveness of enforcement action where breaches occur.

The bill will address this risk by introducing group accountability provisions. This will make sure enforcement action reflects the economic reality of corporate structures, so that those with real control over a building cannot avoid responsibility through complex ownership arrangements.

These provisions will allow for a regulator to serve a penalty notice for certain offenses (failure to remediate, obstruction and costs for a Remediation Management Order) on both the corporate responsible entity and any firms that exercise control of them and would be named on the Remediation Compliance Statement. Any companies jointly served a penalty notice will be jointly responsible for paying the fine.

The government intends for these powers to only be used in the most egregious cases, and where it is clear that serving a notice only on the responsible entity would fail to capture those who were responsible for a failure to remediate. We will publish guidance for regulators making this clear after the passage of the bill.

The government recognises that these powers are far reaching and interact with the principles of corporate limited liability. However, given the scale of building safety issues and the risk to life where they remain unremediated, the powers are necessary to ensure that there are clear and effective sanctions on those who fail to take appropriate steps.

These powers are time limited and will be reviewed on a regular basis by both the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) and the Department for Business Innovation, Science and Trade to make sure they remain fit for purpose.

Implementation of the legal duty to remediate

The legal duties to assess, mitigate and remediate will come into force 2 months after Royal Assent.

Ahead of this, MHCLG will publish draft guidance to help responsible entities understand their legal obligations with regards to assessing their buildings in advance of the assessment deadline, including how FRAEWs must be carried out and audited, and remediating their buildings as soon as reasonably practicable. Guidance will be issued before those powers come into force to support regulators in exercising their functions. This will include guidance on calculating variable monetary penalties and on the use of retained fine monies to cover the cost of certain prescribed enforcement actions connected to the legal duties. This guidance will come into force as statutory guidance alongside the duties soon after Royal Assent.

Regulations will be published setting out what may be considered ‘required remediation steps’ and ‘tolerable remediation’ for the purpose of complying with the duty to remediate. These will come into force 2 months after Royal Assent alongside the new legal duties.

The strengthened powers for regulators to enforce compliance with the mitigation and remediation duties will come into force alongside the duties 2 months after Royal Assent. From the assessment and remediation compliance plan deadlines, 12 and 15 months after Royal Assent respectively, regulators will be able to take enforcement action for failure to comply with those duties.

Will leaseholders have to pay additional costs for the legal duty to remediate?

There is government funding in place for all work required by the legal duty to remediate – meaning that leaseholders should not pay towards the cost of remediation conducted under this duty.

What if there are concerns with the quality of an FRAEW produced under the legal duty to remediate?

The bill is designed to make sure FRAEWs carried out under the legal duty to remediate are consistent, high-quality and clearly identify the cladding remediation a building needs. This includes mandatory independent auditing of assessments. All FRAEWs that recommend remediation will be audited, and – for the first time – a proportion of FRAEWs that conclude no remediation is necessary.

Residents who have concerns about the safety of their building can already raise this through Homes England’s ‘Tell Us’ tool. They may also be able to raise concerns with their local regulator, who has powers to investigate where appropriate.

Will a responsible entity be compliant with the duty to remediate if their building is in interim measures?

Interim measures – such as waking watch patrols – are temporary mitigations. They are not an acceptable long-term alternative to permanent remediation because their costs are disproportionate compared with long-term measures and their long-term use adversely impacts residents and local regulators.

To be compliant with the legal duty to remediate, responsible entities must carry out the works recommended in FRAEW to make their buildings sustainably safe. Buildings put in interim measures to support a temporary change in evacuation strategy, must be remediated so that the interim measures can be stood down.

Will right to manage companies and resident management companies be subject to penalties under the legal duty to remediate?

The department is committed to supporting Right to Manage Companies (RTMs) and Resident Management Companies (RMCs) in delivering their responsibilities. We recognise that many are volunteer-led organisations and that the building safety and remediation landscape can be complex to navigate.

That is why the bill is accompanied by a package of measures designed to provide clarity and support. We will make regulations setting out the remediation steps required to comply with the legal duty to remediate, supported by statutory guidance on when those steps should be taken. Together with wider guidance, this will provide a clear compliance roadmap, helping RTMs and RMCs understand what is expected of them and reducing uncertainty about their obligations.

The purpose of the bill is to drive action where responsible entities are failing to remediate unsafe cladding, not to penalise those who are making genuine efforts to comply. Regulators are expected under the Regulators’ Code to support compliance through advice, guidance and engagement where appropriate, and the legal duty to remediate is intended to focus enforcement on persistent inaction and poor behaviour rather than resident-led organisations that are taking reasonable steps to progress remediation.

Where enforcement action is required, there are important safeguards to ensure it remains fair and proportionate. Regulators must take account of the circumstances of each case, including whether there is a reasonable excuse for any failure to comply, such as delays arising from factors outside a responsible entity’s control. In addition, before imposing a financial penalty on a leaseholder-controlled company, regulators will be required to have regard to statutory guidance, including on whether alternative enforcement tools may be more appropriate. Together, these measures help ensure that enforcement is targeted at those failing to meet their responsibilities, while protecting those acting responsibly to make their buildings safe.

The Remediation Backstop

Overview

Relevant duty-holders have always been responsible for making their buildings safe from fire safety risks. Where they do not, fines and penalties can be a suitable sanction.

However, these sanctions do not guarantee the building will be fixed. The Remediation Backstop will operate as a final safety net where existing enforcement and available funding have not resulted in the building’s duty-holder (the person who is obliged to repair it) carrying out necessary remediation works. The existing duty-holder may have failed to comply with enforcement action taken against them, or with the legal duty to remediate. In these circumstances, local authorities or Homes England (remediation authorities) may be able to carry out the required remediation works instead.

To carry out these works, remediation authorities will be allowed to access funds from the government remediation schemes. Remediation authorities may also be able to apply for short-term assistance to meet additional administrative and legal costs associated with the backstop. These additional costs will then be recoverable from duty-holders once remediation has been completed.

Use of the Remediation Backstop

Examples of compliance failures which could trigger the backstop include:

a notice requiring removal or alteration of offending work under section 36 of the Building Act 1984

an Improvement Notice served by local authorities under the Housing Act 2004

an Enforcement Notice served by the local fire and rescue authority under the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005

a Compliance Notice served under sections 99 to 100 of the Building Safety Act 2022 or section 36 of the Building Act 1984

a Remediation Order issued by the First-tier Tribunal (FTT) under the Building Safety Act 2022

a failure to comply with the legal duty to remediate

Where the duty-holder does not comply with a notice, an order, or the legal duty to remediate, the relevant regulator will be able to choose to take further punitive action, such as issuing fines or seeking a prosecution. Where the regulator believes there is no realistic path to remediation by the current duty-holder, it will be able to refer the case to the relevant local authority or to Homes England (as the designated ‘remediation authorities’) to consider a Remediation Management Order.

Where the remediation authority believes that a building might be suitable for the backstop, it will need to first serve a remediation notice on the duty-holder.

The notice will give the duty-holder 3 months to provide information about any steps it has already taken towards remediating life-critical external wall defects. The notice will also allow 3 months for the duty-holder (and other relevant persons who received the notice) to provide representations as to why they believe the backstop should not be considered for the building.

If the remediation authority decides to proceed with the backstop, it will need to apply to an FTT for a Remediation Management Order.

Remediation Management Orders

If the tribunal makes a Remediation Management Order, the remediation authority will be given powers to carry out the remedial works.

For its duration, a Remediation Management Order will allow the remediation authority to do anything that the duty-holder could ordinarily do for the purpose of assessing and remediating the external walls. For instance, the remediation authority will likely be granted access rights and the rights to deal with third parties (for example, by managing and entering into contracts) when necessary. The Order may also suspend the powers of the duty-holder.

While the Order is in force, the remediation authority may have some responsibility for managing the building on a day-to-day basis, depending on the terms. This means that, in addition to undertaking remediation work, the remediation authority may also be responsible for ensuring that some of the building services continue to operate whilst the Order is in place.

No fixed timescale for the Order will be prescribed by the tribunal. Once the works recommended by the FRAEW have been completed, a post-works assessment will be conducted. Provided this is satisfactory, the remediation authority will be expected to apply to the tribunal to discharge the Order, and the management of the building will revert to the control of the duty-holder.

Cost recovery

The remediation authority will cover the cost of remediation work through existing government remediation schemes. The duty-holder will be expected to repay additional costs incurred as a result of a Remediation Management Order where these were not covered by existing funds. All such repayable costs are expected to attract interest.

Once the works and the post-works assessment of the building are complete, the remediation authority will serve a costs notice on the duty-holder. This will create a debt for the recoverable sums that must be paid by a set time. The duty-holder will be able to repay the costs in full, arrange to repay the costs through a payment plan, or appeal the sum. If the costs notice is appealed, it will take effect only after the appeal is resolved.

A costs notice will automatically be registered as a local land charge where the duty-holder can be shown to have a legal interest in the building – for example, where the duty-holder is the freeholder of the property or holds a superior lease. This charge will carry with it a power of sale. This means that where the debt is not paid, the remediation authority may choose to sell the duty-holder’s interest in the building and use any proceeds to recover the debt. Once a duty-holder pays the debt in full, the charge will be removed. The remediation authority would not be allowed to ‘profit’ from the sale of any property interest.

Where a duty-holder does not respond to the demand notice or its response is not satisfactory, the remediation authority may choose to recover costs in other ways. For example, in addition to enforcing the sale of the duty-holder’s property interest, the tribunal may direct that rent or rent-related payments that would normally be payable to the duty-holder are instead payable to the remediation authority, and that this can continue for debt recovery purposes.

None of the above will remove the right of a remediation authority to obtain a court judgement for the debt, which the duty-holder would be required to pay. The remediation authority could seek to enforce this judgement where payment was not made.

Implementation of the Remediation Backstop

Around 6 months after Royal Assent of the bill, the government will issue secondary legislation setting out how notices should be given to those listed in the legislation. We will also issue guidance on how remediation authorities are expected to use their powers under a Remediation Management Order.

The government will work with remediation authorities to establish a clear framework for interventions.

My building may be applicable for the backstop. What should I do?

If you are a leaseholder or resident and are concerned that remediation work is not progressing, you should first raise this with the organisation responsible for managing the building and, where appropriate, your local regulator.

Remediation Management Orders are intended for situations where those responsible for remediating unsafe cladding have failed to take the action required of them. A building may become eligible for consideration where, for example:

a duty-holder has failed to comply with a statutory notice requiring remedial works

a duty-holder has failed to comply with a Remediation Order approved by the FTT or

a duty-holder has failed to take reasonable and practicable steps to meet the legal duty to remediate

Where a building is referred to a remediation authority for consideration of a Remediation Management Order, the remediation authority must first notify the duty-holder and give them an opportunity to explain why the backstop would not be appropriate or proportionate. Leaseholders and other affected parties will also be notified and given an opportunity to make representations before any decision is made.

Won’t responsible entities just allow their buildings to be subject to the backstop if it is an option?

Where the backstop has been used, regulators will still be able to prosecute the responsible entity for failure to comply with prior enforcement and the legal duty to remediate.

The backstop forms part of a package and is not an alternative to prosecution or fines.

The backstop also requires the responsible entity to pay for all management and legal costs associated with the backstop, which are costs that it would not need to pay for if it carried out the remediation works itself.

Will any costs of the Remediation Backstop be passed on to leaseholders?

Leaseholders will continue to be protected from unfair costs. The Building Safety Act 2022 introduced strict limits on what leaseholders can be charged for the remediation of historical fire safety defects in buildings over 11 metres. Those protections will continue to apply under the Remediation Backstop. This means that qualifying leaseholders will continue to benefit from the protections provided by the Building Safety Act 2022, and should not generally face new or additional costs because a Remediation Management Order has been used to deliver cladding remediation.

Will local authorities and Homes England have the capacity to undertake this work?

The Remediation Backstop is designed to allow local authorities and Homes England to take a flexible approach to the management of the building, which should mitigate some capacity pressures.

We expect that the backstop will primarily be operated by Homes England through a centralised approach, and that third parties can be contracted to undertake works and management of the building. This builds on Homes England’s existing approach to offer technical support for buildings in the Cladding Safety Scheme.

Homes England will be able to act as a Remediation Authority across England, including in London. The Mayor of London has agreed that Homes England should exercise these functions directly in London and not through delegation. This arrangement is limited to the specific functions established by the bill for the Remediation Backstop and does not affect or delegate any other Mayoral functions or responsibilities in the Greater London area.

Regulator co-operation

Overview

In England, there are 3 regulators with distinct but overlapping duties to regulate fire safety risks in domestic properties: local authorities, fire and rescue authorities and the Building Safety Regulator. Co-operation is therefore essential for effective regulation.

To support more efficient and co-ordinated enforcement, the bill will strengthen how regulators work together. It will introduce a clear, overarching duty on regulators to co-operate and co-ordinate, so there is no ambiguity about which organisation is leading on investigation or enforcement at specific buildings with fire safety risks.

The Building Safety Regulator will be required to publish a Regulatory Co-operation Statement within 8 months of commencement, following consultation with local authorities and fire and rescue authorities. This will formalise how the Building Safety Regulator will co-operate with local authorities and fire and rescue authorities at a national level.

To support co-ordinated action locally, the bill will also require local authorities and fire and rescue authorities in the same area to put in place partnership working agreements. These must be in place within 4 months of the Building Safety Regulator’s Regulatory Co-operation Statement being published and will set out how regulators will work together to enforce remediation, including who leads on investigation and enforcement, how information is shared, and how disputes are resolved.

There will be a single partnership working agreement between all local authorities and fire and rescue authorities in Mayoral Strategic Authorities. Outside of Mayoral Strategic Authority areas, agreements will need to be between the local authorities and fire and rescue authorities that share overlapping geographic remits.

To assist data sharing between regulators, the bill will also introduce a data-sharing requirement. Local authorities, fire and rescue authorities, the Building Safety Regulator, and Mayoral Strategic Authorities will be required to share information with each other and MHCLG upon request. This will allow regulators to access the information they need quickly to support enforcement.

In addition to improving co-operation, we are introducing powers to support relevant authorities to deliver their remediation duties under the bill. The bill will grant the Secretary of State the power to issue statutory guidance to local authorities, fire and rescue authorities and the Building Safety Regulator, which they must follow when exercising their relevant functions to enforce remediation. This will set clear expectations on how regulators should carry out their existing and new functions.

Statutory directions

The bill will give the Secretary of State the power to issue statutory directions to all enforcing authorities regarding issues on a national level, or a certain type of enforcing authority. For example, Secretary of State can use this power to issue directions to all fire and rescue authorities, or all local authorities. This power will only be used to direct the Building Safety Regulator if it applies to them in the same way as other authorities. This can be used in circumstances where the Secretary of State needs to quickly communicate changes in strategic direction and make sure all regulators are aligned.

The Remediation Bill will also grant the Secretary of State the power to issue targeted statutory directions to one or more regulators. This separate direction power will not apply to the Building Safety Regulator. For example, these directions could direct 2 local regulators to review their partnership working agreements and procedure, where co-operation is identified as a barrier to effective enforcement.

Implementation of regulator co-operation

All the regulator co-operation measures will come into force 2 months after Royal Assent of the bill.

From commencement, Secretary of State will have the power to issue statutory guidance to regulators regarding their remediation enforcement functions. For example, this could cover how to enforce the legal duty to remediate, co-operation and accountability measures and any other matters the Secretary of State thinks is necessary.

How will these measures improve remediation?

The measures support more efficient and co-ordinated enforcement action, by strengthening how regulators work together. Regulators will be required to share information and co-ordinate action, helping ensure unsafe buildings are not missed and avoiding duplication. Overall, this will support quicker, more effective action to get unsafe buildings fixed.

Will local authorities, fire and rescue services, and the building safety regulator still be able to take joint action?

These proposals still allow for regulators to take joint action where appropriate.

The Regulatory Co-operation Statement and partnership working agreements should set out circumstances where joint action may be sought.

What can an enforcement body do if their local partner isn’t working collaboratively with them?

Disagreements should be resolved locally through senior level engagement. To assist this, the partnership working agreements – and the Building Safety Regulator’s Regulatory Co-operation Statement – will be required to contain dispute resolution arrangements.

Where there are ongoing co-operation issues between bodies - which have not been resolved through local engagement - then the Secretary of State may consider issuing a direction, but this would be a last resort.

Will the partnership working agreements duplicate measures already outline in Local Remediation Acceleration Plans?

Some areas already have partnership working agreements, Local Remediation Acceleration Plans, protocols or memorandums of understanding in place.

Where joint working agreements are already in place, local authorities and fire and rescue authorities should assess existing arrangements, and make sure they meet the requirements set out in the bill and any accompanying guidance.

Construction product manufacturer redress: section 149

Overview

Section 149 of the Building Safety Act 2022 allows legal action to be brought against manufacturers of cladding products where those products have caused or contributed to a building being unfit for habitation and in need of remediation.

To establish liability, a claimant must show that a product was defective, failed to meet regulatory requirements, or was sold on the basis of misleading statements, and that its use caused the building to be unsafe. Claims are brought by those with a legal interest in the building, such as owners or leaseholders.

Section 149 has not worked as intended. Very few claims have been made and stakeholders report that the regime is complex, difficult to evidence, and too easily allows liability to be avoided in practice. Current problems with section 149 include:

it is difficult to prove liability in cases involving multiple products

manufacturers can rely on technical compliance arguments, even where products contributed to unsafe outcomes

there is no clear route for some parties in the construction sector, such as developers, to bring direct claims against manufacturers where they have funded remediation due to unsafe or mis‑sold products

As a result, many of those who acted to fix unsafe buildings have borne the costs themselves, while manufacturers are not contributing.

The bill will make it easier for those who have paid to fix unsafe buildings to recover those costs from the manufacturers responsible by simplifying the section 149 statutory conditions.

First, the bill will place a clearer focus on safety and conduct. Liability will now turn on whether a product was unsafe or whether there was misleading conduct, rather than narrow technical compliance arguments about defectiveness.

Second, the causation test will also be simplified. It will be enough to show that a product made more than a trivial contribution to a building being unsafe.

Third, developers and others who have funded remediation will be able to bring claims directly against manufacturers.

The bill will also confirm that courts can apply Building Liability Orders to section 149 claims, allowing liability to be extended to associated companies where it is just and equitable. Courts will also be able to require companies to provide relevant product information to support claims.

Together, these changes will ensure that those who have been affected by unsafe and mis-sold cladding products have a clear route to recover costs, and that responsibility for remediation is shared more fairly across those who contributed to the problem.

Section 149 will continue to operate through the civil courts. Where liability is established, courts may require manufacturers to pay damages, including the costs of remediation linked to their products.

Implementation of construction product manufacturer redress: section 149

The changes will come into force 2 months after Royal Assent. They will apply to new claims and to cases already underway at that point, within the existing 30-year limitation period under the Building Safety Act 2022. These reforms will apply UK-wide, bringing Northern Ireland into scope for the first time.

No secondary legislation or statutory guidance is planned.

Will making it easier to bring claims lead to manufacturers becoming insolvent?

The reforms do not create automatic liability or guarantee claims will be successful. All claims must still be tested and proven through the courts, and will arise only where a manufacturer’s products have contributed to building safety failures.

The intention is not to penalise responsible businesses, but to ensure that those who supplied unsafe or mis‑sold products are held accountable.

Will this slow down remediation?

The reforms are designed to support remediation. The changes will create a better route to recover costs after remediation has taken place. Parties cannot rely on potential claims to defer or avoid their responsibility to remediate.

Developers and others who have committed to fix buildings, including through the Developer Remediation Contract, remain expected to do so. That position is unchanged. This provision is about how costs are recovered.

Medium-rise (11 to 18 metre) building register

Overview

The Building Safety Act 2022 required the Building Safety Regulator to create a register of 18 metres plus residential buildings – defined in the act as ‘higher-risk buildings’. This means the government should now have a complete record of higher-risk buildings in England, making it easier to identify those with potentially unsafe cladding.

However, even though they are within scope of government funding programmes for unsafe cladding, no comparative register exists for medium-rise buildings (also described as 11 to 18 metre buildings).

The Cladding Safety Scheme’s review of Ordnance Survey data has identified the vast majority, but not all, medium-rise buildings in England. This means buildings with potentially dangerous cladding may not be found via this approach.

The bill will give the Secretary of State the power to create a register of occupied ‘medium-rise buildings’. Medium-rise buildings means residential buildings in England with 2 or more dwellings, that are between 11 and 18 metres tall, or which have at least 5 storeys but fewer than 7.

The ‘registration duty-holder’ will have to register the building, provide key details about it, and pay a registration charge. A registration duty-holder is an organisation or individual who owns or has a legal obligation to repair any common parts of the building. Where there is more than one party meeting these criteria, then whoever owns or has a legal obligation to repair the structure and exterior of the building will be the registration duty-holder.

Failing to register, provide or update the required information will be subject to civil penalties of up to £7,000, with higher financial penalties of up to £40,000 or prosecution available if the non-compliance continues. Knowingly providing wrong or deliberately misleading information will be an offence liable to prosecution. Any prosecutions will be in the magistrates’ court and may result in an unlimited fine and/or (in the case of the provision of false or misleading information) a custodial sentence up to the general limit in the magistrates’ court.

Implementation of the medium-rise building register

The medium-rise building register requirements will come into force once the necessary secondary legislation has been laid. We anticipate this will be approximately 8 to 10 months after Royal Assent. The secondary legislation will specify important information relating to the operation of the register, including:

the operational remit of the body appointed to be the registrar (if not the Secretary of State)

the specific building information required for registration

the registration fee or charges

the deadline for initial registration

What will be the cost to register?

There will be an upfront registration charge, calculated with reference to the costs of establishing and operating the register. The charge will be set out in secondary legislation, but we anticipate it will be similar, or lower, than the charge levied by the Building Safety Regulator for registering a higher-risk building which is currently £251.

As with higher-risk buildings, registration costs (including the charge and any costs of complying with registration requirements) will be recoverable from leaseholders through the service charge. However, the process for medium-rise buildings is much lighter-touch, meaning costs for the 11 to 18 metre register should be significantly lower than those under the full higher-risk buildings regime.

Will the register be made publicly available? Will leaseholders and residents be able to access it?

Yes but, as for the higher-risk building register, in a limited way. The intention is for the medium-rise building register to be searchable by postcode so that residents and leaseholders can see if their building is registered.

We expect that, at a minimum, the same high-level information as for higher-risk buildings will be made publicly available, namely: building details (height, floors, residential units, date of completion) and the registration duty-holder (though not their contact details.)

Beneficial ownership

Overview

Some residential blocks are owned through companies, partnerships, trusts or similar arrangements. In these cases, it may not be clear from the legal title alone who ultimately owns or controls the building, or who is connected to it. This can make it challenging for regulators trying to enforce remediation to identify the right parties to engage with and, where necessary, take enforcement action against

The bill will give certain public authorities a power to require building ownership information for residential blocks in England. For these purposes, a residential block is a self-contained building, or self-contained part of a building, containing at least 2 dwellings.

The authorities who will be able to use this power are:

local housing authorities

fire and rescue authorities

the Building Safety Regulator

Homes England

The information that may be required includes information that appears useful for:

finding out whether the legal owner of the whole or part of the block is a body corporate or partnership

identifying beneficial owners connected with that owner

identifying people associated with that owner or beneficial owner

understanding the relationship those people have with the building

The bill will create summary offences for failing to comply with a notice and for deliberately providing false or misleading information. A person convicted of failing to comply with a notice will be liable to a fine or authorities may instead impose a financial penalty of up to £40,000. A person convicted of knowingly or recklessly providing false or misleading information will be liable to imprisonment or a fine, or both.

Information provided under a notice may be shared between relevant authorities and used by them in connection with their building safety functions.

Implementation of beneficial ownership

The new powers will become available to relevant authorities following Royal Assent. Guidance and training will be developed to support implementation and effective use of the powers covering. This may cover, for example:

when and how to issue building ownership information notices

how to handle complex cases (for example, involving trusts or offshore entities)

best practice for monitoring compliance and escalating to enforcement where necessary

How will this help enforcement?

It will give relevant authorities a clearer understanding of who they are dealing with, allowing them to take a more strategic approach to enforcement. For example, knowing that a building is owned by a company that is part of a wider corporate group may affect how a relevant authority approaches engagement and enforcement and, consequently, may help to speed up remediation.

How will this help leaseholders?

Building ownership information notices should help relevant authorities act more quickly and effectively by making it easier to identify who ultimately owns and controls a building, particularly where ownership is obscured by complex structures. That can support more targeted enforcement and engagement, help reduce delays, and ultimately help to speed up remediation.

Amendments to previous legislation

Decants

Where a serious hazard or fire safety risk is found in a residential building, the enforcing authority may prohibit occupation of all or part of the building to protect people from harm. That can mean residents having to leave their homes until the risk has been addressed. This is known as a ‘decant’.

Decants have serious impacts on residents so, where unavoidable, duration should be minimised.

The bill will make sure that that prohibitions are paired with enforcement action that requires critical safety works to be undertaken by a set deadline, helping to ensure that residents can return to their homes as soon as possible.

The amendments will stipulate that, where a local housing authority initiates a decant by making a prohibition order under the Housing Act 2004 and considers that action can be taken to make the building safe for occupation, it must also serve an improvement notice requiring that action. In the case of an emergency prohibition order, the improvement notice must be served within 28 days.

Similarly, where a fire and rescue authority serves a prohibition notice in relation to a risk in a relevant building under the Fire Safety Order and considers that action can be taken to make the building safe for occupation, it must issue an enforcement notice within 28 days.

These changes will ensure that, where a building is unsafe, prohibiting its use goes hand-in-hand with enforcement action requiring critical safety works to be done as quickly as possible. This should minimise the amount of time residents are forced to spend out of their homes.

How is the new policy going to ensure these buildings are fixed as quickly as possible?

By requiring fire and rescue authorities and local authorities to issue enforcement or improvement notices alongside prohibition notices and orders, we will place a clear, enforceable legal duty on responsible entities to address critical safety defects within defined timeframes.

This will help to prevent unnecessarily long decants, meaning residents can return to their homes more quickly.

Will regulators still be able to make decisions based on individual circumstances?

Regulators will retain the ability to exercise their discretion and will only be required to issue improvement and enforcement notices alongside a prohibition where it is reasonably practicable for action to be taken to reduce the risk level. For example, it would not improve resident experiences to require regulators to serve an improvement or enforcement notice in scenarios where a building is at the end of its life and due to be demolished.

At the same time, the policy framework is designed to promote greater consistency, ensuring that enforcement action is taken in the majority of cases. This approach strikes a balance between protecting tailored, case-by-case decision-making and delivering a more predictable and effective enforcement regime.

Remediation Order enforcement and related amendments

Remediation Orders are orders made by a tribunal on the application of an interested person (such as leaseholders) which require a landlord to carry out remediation work within a specified time frame.

The bill will strengthen the enforcement framework for Remediation Orders, by making provision for regulations to introduce civil financial penalties. This will enable a direct enforcement mechanism for a civil financial penalty to be imposed, providing a clear route for those looking to enforce sanctions for non-compliance.

In England, this will enable regulations to provide the FTT to impose civil financial penalties of up to £500,000 where a landlord has failed to comply with a Remediation Order. Successive penalties may be imposed where there is continued non-compliance. The bill also includes provision to enable a corresponding enforcement framework to be established for Remediation Orders in Wales.

The measure will also allow a requirement for information and documents to be provided, for the purposes of monitoring compliance with Remediation Orders, with further details to be set out in regulations. This may include, for example, information about the progress and timing of remediation works. Financial penalties, up to a maximum of £40,000, may be imposed for failure to comply with this requirement.

These arrangements will operate alongside existing enforcement mechanisms, rather than replace them. The measure will apply to both new and existing Remediation Orders, made before the provisions come into effect, but only where there is continuing non-compliance.

The bill will also clarify that no limitation period under the Limitation Act 1980 applies to Remediation Orders, Remediation Contribution Orders and Building Liability Orders. Corresponding provision is made in relation to Wales.

This will provide certainty as to the availability of these remedies and help ensure that unsafe buildings can be remediated and that leaseholders and other interested persons can continue to access these protections.

The provisions for England will come into force 2 months following Royal Assent of the bill, and the detailed operation of the regime, will be set out in secondary legislation. Separate provision is made in relation to Wales.

Why is the penalty set at a maximum of £500,000?

The £500,000 cap is designed to strike a balance between providing a strong deterrent and ensuring proportionality in individual cases, with the tribunal retaining discretion to set the penalty. This allows the tribunal to flexibility impose higher penalties, within the £500,000 cap, in more serious cases.

Importantly, this is not a one-off penalty as landlords are still expected to comply with the original Remediation Order. Where a landlord continues to fail to comply with a Remediation Order, successive penalties can be imposed by the tribunal.

Protecting Remediation Contribution Order funds in trust

Remediation Contribution Orders were introduced under the Building Safety Act 2022 to make sure residents, local authorities and regulators can obtain funding to fix building safety defects through a court order requiring liable parties (developers and/or persons associated with them) to pay. However, there are no controls on how these funds are held. If a recipient (for example, a landlord) subsequently entered insolvency proceedings, Remediation Contribution Order remediation funds could be distributed to creditors as a priority under insolvency law. This creates a risk that funds may not be used for the purposes specified in the Order and that remediation is not accomplished. Because a Remediation Contribution Order represents the settlement of a claim, leaseholders will not be able to bring a further claim against the same party in future.

This measure will require Remediation Contribution Order to be held in a trust. The trust will protect remediation funds for remediation of building safety defects and ensure they are used for the purposes intended, even if a recipient, such as the landlord, obtains the funds and then subsequently becomes insolvent.

This new requirement will come into force shortly after royal assent by way of commencement regulations, to allow time for relevant changes to be made to the civil procedure rules and practice directions for the courts. We will also publish guidance for trustees on how to establish and manage the trust funds.

Who can be a trustee and what is their role?

The Remediation Contribution Order applicant may decide that the company or individual responsible for repairing the building (freeholder, management company, or head lessee) is best placed to act as the trustee of funds.

The trustee will be responsible for holding the sums in a trust fund for the purpose of making the payments referred to in the order.

How much will the trusts cost applicants?

We will provide that the First-tier Tribunal can award costs for establishing the trust account as part of the Remediation Contribution Order. If for any reason funds are not sufficient, it would be open to the applicants to return to the tribunal to request that they vary the order.

Notification of regulators

The insolvency of a Responsible Person can have implications for the safe management of a building which is subject to the Building Safety Act or Fire Safety Order regimes. Section 125A of the Building Safety Act 2022 (as amended by section 119 of the Leasehold and Freehold Reform Act 2024) puts a duty on Insolvency Practitioners who are appointed to the insolvency of a Responsible Person for a residential building, which is at least 5 storeys or 11 metres plus high, to notify local regulators (local authorities and fire and rescue services). In the case of higher-risk buildings (buildings which are at least 7 storeys or 18 metres plus in height), the Building Safety Regulator must also be notified. This ensures regulators are aware of the situation and can, at their discretion engage with both the Insolvency Practitioner and/or residents to check that the building is being safely managed during insolvency proceedings.

The Bill will extend this notification requirement to 2 further possible types of insolvency:

voluntary arrangements (an agreement to pay off some or all of their debts through an insolvency professional)

moratorium (a temporary timeframe giving an entity immunity from creditors to plan their financial affairs)

The Bill will require Responsible Persons for buildings of 11 metres or more in height who enter into voluntary arrangements or moratoriums to notify relevant regulators within 14 calendar days. They will need to provide high-level details about themselves, their financial situation, and the relevant building or buildings for which they are the Responsible Person.

Landlord liquidations and disclaimers

The liquidation of an Accountable Person under the Building Safety Act regime, or a Responsible Person under the Fire Safety Order, can also have implications for the safe management of buildings. When a landlord is liquidated, a ‘legal estate’ they hold in the common parts of a building (for example, a freehold or headlease) may be disclaimed. This may affect the ongoing management, maintenance or remediation of the building. The leases and leaseholders remain, but leaseholders may not have the necessary rights to carry out works to the common parts of the building. This may expose leaseholders to building safety risks because they may be unable to progress key maintenance or remediation works.

The Bill introduces a requirement on Insolvency Practitioners to notify local regulators (local authorities and fire and rescue services) within 7 business days when disclaiming a ‘relevant interest’ in a residential building that is 11 metres or above in height. A relevant interest means a legal estate (that is, a freehold or leasehold interest recognised in law, such as a headlease) in any part of the common parts of the building. In the case of higher-risk buildings (buildings which are at least 7 storeys or 18 metres or more in height) the Building Safety Regulator must also be notified. Insolvency Practitioners must notify regulators by sending them a copy of the ‘notice of disclaimer’.This will ensure regulators are aware of the situation and may, at their discretion, engage with the Insolvency Practitioner and/or residents to check the building is being safely managed.

We expect the measures on notification of landlord insolvency and disclaimer to come into effect 2 months after Royal Assent of the bill.

How will this improve resident safety?

The new notification requirements will ensure that local authorities and fire and rescue authorities and/or the Building Safety Regulator are made aware of relevant insolvency and disclaimer events and can, at their discretion, engage with the Insolvency Practitioner, landlord and/or leaseholders to check that the building is being managed appropriately and that leaseholders are safe. This will apply either when the Responsible Person of a building that is 11 metres or more in height enters a relevant insolvency process, or where an Insolvency Practitioner disclaims a ‘relevant interest’, meaning a legal estate (a freehold or leasehold interest recognised in law, such as a headlease) in any part of the common parts of the building.

Section 24 managers in the higher-risk buildings regime

Under the Building Safety Act 2022, building safety duties for higher-risk buildings must be carried out by an ‘Accountable Person’. Where a manager is appointed under section 24 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1987, that manager may take over the management of the building, but is not currently treated as the Accountable Person and cannot carry out building safety duties under the act. This means that responsibility for building safety duties can remain with the landlord, even where they are no longer managing the building.

The bill intends to change the Building Safety Act 2022 so that, where a manager is appointed under a section 24 order, they can be treated as the Accountable Person for a higher-risk building where they meet the definition under the act. In practice, this will allow them to take on responsibility for building safety, alongside other management responsibilities. It also allows the Building Safety Regulator to deal directly with the manager, for example in relation to submitting safety cases.

These changes apply to both new and existing section 24 orders and are intended to ensure that responsibility for building safety duties sits with the person managing the building.

The measure will come into force 2 months after Royal Assent.

Will section 24 managers be subject to enforcement action or liability?

Where a section 24 manager becomes the Accountable Person, they will be subject to the same regulatory and legal framework as other Accountable Persons. This includes the possibility of enforcement action by the Building Safety Regulator, as well as potential criminal liability if they fail to comply with their duties. Decisions on enforcement, including whether to take prosecution action, will be made by the Building Safety Regulator in line with its existing, proportionate approach.

How will this support building remediation?

This will support remediation by addressing a gap in the current framework, where a section 24 manager can be appointed to replace a failing landlord but may lack the powers needed to progress remediation, as responsibility remains with the building owner.

Appointment of section 24 manager or acquisition of right to nanage in escheat or bona vacantia

Escheat is the common law process by which freehold land in England and Wales, which has become ‘ownerless’, returns to the Crown with the freehold title destroyed. Bona vacantia is property which passes to the Crown when a company is dissolved. These can happen, for example, where a landlord becomes insolvent and liquidates. Where this affects a residential building with leaseholders, they will often be left without a landlord/freeholder who has the rights to manage and repair the common parts of the building. This can create serious problems with repairs, maintenance, service charge collection and general compliance with legal duties. Leaseholders may find themselves legally unable to maintain or remediate the common parts of the building. They will also be unable to apply to government remediation funds.

The bill will address this by making clear that existing legal routes for taking over or securing management of a building can be used where the premises have become subject to escheat or bona vacantia.

One route is the right to manage (RTM). This measure will make it clear that leaseholders can apply to acquire the RTM, where eligible, where the premises have become subject to escheat or bona vacantia. The other route is the appointment of a court-appointed manager under section 24 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1987. This measure will make it clear that a tribunal can appoint a section 24 manager where the premises have become subject to escheat or bona vacantia.

This is intended to help leaseholders keep their building safe and maintained, and where relevant, support further steps towards remediation.

These changes will come into effect 2 months after Royal Assent. The department intends to publish accompanying guidance to support leaseholders.

How does this improve the process of remediation for residents in premises subject to escheat or bona vacantia?

By providing clear legal routes for leaseholders to acquire the RTM or to have a section 24 manager appointed when their premises have become subject to escheat or bona vacantia, leaseholders will be able to make provision for management and maintenance of the common parts of the building, including the collection of service charges. This will help ensure that the building is managed safely, allowing leaseholders to remain safe in their homes while they seek to access remediation funding, where appropriate.

I’m in a building that has become subject to escheat. What can I do?

Leaseholders can form a RTM company and acquire the right to manage or make an application to the FTT for the appointment of a section 24 manager. This measure will make clear that these routes can be pursued where the premises is subject to escheat or bona vacantia.

Leaseholders should take independent legal advice to confirm which route they should pursue. However, where leaseholders are unable to form a RTM company (for example, because they do not meet the participation requirements), they may apply to the FTT to seek to have a section 24 manager appointed instead.

Residential Personal Emergency Evacuation Plans

The Fire Safety (Residential Evacuation Plans) (England) Regulations 2025 implement a package of measures to support residents who may have difficulty evacuating in a fire. The regulations apply to individuals living in high-rise residential buildings (with 7 or more stories or 18 metres plus in height), or in those medium-rise residential buildings (over 11 metres in height) operating a Simultaneous Evacuation strategy. The regulations place duties on the Responsible Person (usually the building owner or manager) to identify and assess the needs of relevant residents through a person-centred fire risk assessment (PCFRA), and to put in place reasonable measures to support their safety. However, these legal duties on the PCFRA are currently limited to the common parts of residential buildings, which limits the ability to fully assess individual risks and potential in-flat mitigations.

The bill addresses this gap by extending the legal duty to carry out the PCFRA to consider the risk within the flats of relevant residents, subject to their consent. This supports a more complete assessment of individual needs and helps ensure appropriate measures can be identified. It will form part of the government’s response to the Grenfell Tower Inquiry and is intended to complete the overall policy framework for Residential Personal Emergency Evacuation Plans (RPEEPs).

The detailed operation of these duties will continue to sit in secondary legislation and statutory guidance, Residential PEEPs: Guidance for Responsible Persons, which will be updated to reflect the changes made by the bill.

What if the resident does not want to engage with RPEEPs or believes it is too intrusive to consider risks in their own flat?

As with all other elements of the RPEEPs process, resident’s consent will be required and can be withdrawn at any time.

Will extending the PCFRA into the flat make the policy more expensive?

Available evidence does not suggest this. Many building owners/managers have found in-flat measures to be the most practical and proportionate way to improve fire safety of their vulnerable residents, and already include consideration of in flat risks and mitigation measures in their assessments. Examples of these measures can be found in the Responsible Persons toolkit, which accompanies the existing legislation and guidance.

Statutory guidance already recommends building owners/managers to incorporate consideration of in-flat risks within their RPEEPs processes.
